title: Arousing
hookLine: waking good states not yet present

cards: Patience with small children. Giving without keeping score. Staying calm when the flight is canceled and the line at the desk is shouting.
People admire these qualities in a friend and wish they had them. They're easy to file under personality: some people got them, some didn't. The suttas file them somewhere else.
The third of the four efforts is about exactly this: bringing into being good qualities that aren't there yet.

teach.b: The text is short: for wholesome states that haven't arisen, one generates desire, makes an effort, rouses energy, and strives for them to arise.

teach.h: CHANDA: THE WISH IS THE FUEL.
teach.b: The first step is desire, chanda: the wish to have the good thing. Buddhism is sometimes summed up as wanting nothing at all. The suttas are more careful.
Wanting to grow in kindness or patience isn't the problem; it's the fuel.

In the next sutta over, the Buddha says what this effort develops: the seven factors of awakening, mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration and equanimity. So how do good states get started?
The Book of Ones, the first section of the Numbered Discourses, keeps coming back to two sparks. One is wise attention: turning the mind toward things in a way that wakes the good.

teach.h: A HABIT BEGINS AS ONE MORNING.
teach.b: The other is good friendship: spending time with people who already have it. You don't grow patience by staring at the word.
You grow it by noticing the small moments where patience is possible, and by being around patient people until it rubs off. Then the honest obstacle: inertia.
The Dhammapada names it, in Max Müller's words: "He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise" will not find the way.
Arousing the good is mostly about starting, small, on one particular morning.

how: Buddhists cultivate wholesome qualities through daily practices such as meditation, chanting, generosity and keeping good company; teachers often stress the spiritual friend, kalyāṇamitta.

o: a prayer asking for good luck
getting excited about a new practice

games.q: waking the good: tap the pairs.
p: turning the mind toward the good
time with people who have it

s: Buddhism teaches that all desire is bad
right effort begins with chanda, the wish for the good.
the Book of Ones names good friendship as a spark for wholesome states
with wise attention, it keeps coming back as what wakes the good.
in this teaching, good qualities are fixed personality
the third effort is about bringing them into being.

games.q: you'd like to become more patient. by today's teaching, what helps most to get it started?
o: notice small chances for patience, and spend time with patient people.
criticize yourself every time you're impatient.
games.why: the Book of Ones points to wise attention and good friendship as the sparks that wake wholesome states not yet present.

practice: Choose one good quality you'd like more of, patience, generosity, courage, and remember one moment, even a tiny one, when you had a little of it: where you were, how it felt in the body.
That's wise attention, turning toward the seed; then picture the smallest way to practice it, just once.

wordCard.voice: Arousing. The third effort: bringing good states into being. The wish for the good, wise attention, and good friends are the sparks.

orig.note: Pali bhāvanā: developing, bringing into being; the name of the third right effort.

carryVoice: Your line: wake the good. The wish for the good is the fuel, not the problem. That's day three hundred eighty-six.
